title: Acute rhinosinusitis (adult)
subject: ophthalmology-ent
setting: Primary care, emergency department, ENT clinic
summary: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral. Diagnose bacterial rhinosinusitis when symptoms persist 10 days or more without improvement or worsen after initial improvement; offer watchful waiting or amoxicillin with or without clavulanate for 5 to 7 days, avoid imaging unless a complication is suspected, and refer orbital or intracranial red flags the same day.

sections.title: Diagnose
items: Acute rhinosinusitis (up to 4 weeks): purulent nasal drainage (anterior or posterior) with nasal obstruction, facial pain-pressure-fullness, or both.

Presumed acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS, AAO-HNS 2025): symptoms persist without improvement for at least 10 days after onset of an upper respiratory infection, or worsen within 10 days after initial improvement (double worsening).
IDSA 2012 adds severe onset: fever 39 °C or higher with purulent nasal discharge or facial pain for 3 to 4 consecutive days at the start of the illness.
Viral rhinosinusitis is far more common: fever early that settles, purulent discharge that appears only after several days, and improvement within 10 days.
Consider a dental (upper molar) source, allergic rhinitis, migraine and other causes of facial pain.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Do not image patients who meet the criteria for acute rhinosinusitis unless a complication or an alternative diagnosis is suspected (AAO-HNS). Plain sinus X-rays do not help.
Suspected orbital or intracranial complication: urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses, orbits and brain, with MRI if intracranial spread is suspected.
Treatment failure or immunocompromise: obtain cultures from the middle meatus under endoscopy or by sinus aspiration, not nasopharyngeal swabs (IDSA).
Check blood glucose in anyone with diabetes, and urgently in anyone with facial numbness, black nasal crusts or palatal discolouration.

sections.title: Symptom relief (viral and bacterial)
items: Analgesics (paracetamol or ibuprofen), nasal saline irrigation and intranasal corticosteroids may relieve symptoms (AAO-HNS options).

Symptoms for 10 days or more: NICE suggests a high-dose intranasal corticosteroid (for example mometasone 200 micrograms twice daily) for 14 days; it may ease symptoms but does not shorten the illness.
Oral or topical decongestants and antihistamines are not recommended for ABRS (IDSA).
Viral rhinosinusitis: no antibiotic. NICE advises that acute sinusitis usually lasts 2 to 3 weeks; return if symptoms worsen rapidly, do not improve, or the patient becomes systemically unwell.

sections.title: ABRS: watchful waiting or antibiotic
items: Offer watchful waiting without antibiotics to adults with uncomplicated ABRS, whatever the severity, provided follow-up is assured; start an antibiotic if symptoms fail to improve or worsen (AAO-HNS 2025).

If an antibiotic is used: amoxicillin with or without clavulanate for 5 to 7 days for most adults (AAO-HNS). IDSA prefers amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg three times daily or 875/125 mg twice daily.

High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (2 g amoxicillin twice daily) when resistance is likely: fever 39 °C or more or threatened complications, age over 65, recent hospitalisation, antibiotics in the past month, immunocompromise, or high local rates of penicillin-resistant pneumococcus (IDSA).

Penicillin allergy: doxycycline, or a third-generation oral cephalosporin with or without clindamycin (AAO-HNS). Keep respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) for those with no alternative.
Macrolides and co-trimoxazole are not recommended for empirical treatment because of pneumococcal resistance (IDSA).

NICE (UK) differs: phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days first line (often as a back-up prescription); co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg three times daily for 5 days if systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications.

sections.title: Treatment failure and follow-up
items: If symptoms worsen, or fail to improve after 3 to 5 days of an appropriate antibiotic, reassess to confirm ABRS, exclude other causes and look for complications; if ABRS is confirmed, change the antibiotic (for example to high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline).
Refer to ENT for recurrent acute rhinosinusitis (4 or more episodes a year) or symptoms lasting 12 weeks or more (chronic rhinosinusitis).

sections.title: Red flags: refer to hospital the same day
items: Orbital: periorbital oedema or redness, displaced eyeball, double vision, ophthalmoplegia, or newly reduced visual acuity.
Intracranial: severe frontal headache, swelling over the frontal bone, signs of meningitis, focal neurological signs or reduced consciousness.
Severe systemic infection or sepsis.

Possible invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis), seen in India especially with uncontrolled diabetes or ketoacidosis, steroid use, neutropenia or transplant: facial pain or numbness, black nasal eschar, palatal necrosis, proptosis or visual loss. Emergency ENT, imaging and antifungal therapy.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate; avoid doxycycline and fluoroquinolones.
Children are outside this adult protocol; IDSA treats paediatric ABRS with amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 to 14 days.
High risk of complications (for example immunosuppression) or systemically very unwell: NICE advises an immediate antibiotic; in diabetes or immunosuppression look actively for fungal disease.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Prescribing antibiotics in the first week of a cold because the discharge is coloured.
Ordering sinus X-rays or CT for uncomplicated sinusitis.
Missing periorbital cellulitis, a dental source or mucormycosis.
Using macrolides or co-trimoxazole as first-line empirical therapy.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally three times daily or 875 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: AAO-HNS first-line option when resistance risk is low.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.dose: 500/125 mg orally three times daily or 875/125 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days; high dose 2 g amoxicillin twice daily
drugs.notes: IDSA preferred; high dose for resistance risk factors.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily or 200 mg once daily for 5 to 7 days

drugs.name: Cefpodoxime
drugs.dose: 200 mg orally twice daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Third-generation cephalosporin option in non-severe penicillin allergy, with or without clindamycin.

drugs.name: Levofloxacin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally once daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Reserve for no alternative: tendinopathy, QT prolongation and dysglycaemia risks. Adjust in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Moxifloxacin
drugs.dose: 400 mg orally once daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Reserve for no alternative; same fluoroquinolone cautions.

drugs.name: Phenoxymethylpenicillin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally four times daily for 5 days
drugs.notes: NICE first choice when an antibiotic is needed.

drugs.name: Mometasone nasal spray
drugs.dose: 200 micrograms (2 sprays of 50 micrograms into each nostril) twice daily for 14 days
drugs.notes: NICE high-dose option (off-label) for symptoms of 10 days or more.
